passage:
Disha, you want that robot chocolate because of the advert, na? Your Nani was fooled once too.
When I was nine, the radio played a song every evening about Laddu Lion toffees. Laddu Lion had adventures, and at the end all the jungle children danced with him. I thought it was a real story, like my school reader.
I saved coins for two weeks. At school I gave toffees to the girls near the water tap, sure they would dance with me. They ate the toffees and went off to skip rope.
I cried to my Papa. He sat me on the step and said, "That song was not a story, Rashmi beti. It was a shopkeeper talking in a lion's voice."
I never forgot it.

qa.q: How long did young Rashmi save coins for the toffees?
qa.a: Rashmi saved coins for two weeks.

qa.q: What did young Rashmi hope would happen when she shared the toffees?
qa.a: Rashmi hoped the girls near the water tap would dance with her like the jungle children, so she expected the toffees to bring friendship and fun.

qa.q: Which moment in the story helped Rashmi understand what she had heard?
qa.a: Her Papa sitting her on the step and explaining that the song was a shopkeeper talking in a lion's voice helped her see it was an advert, not a story.

qa.q: How might the girls near the water tap have seen the toffees?
qa.a: To them the toffees were just a nice treat, not a reason to become closer, which is why they ate them and went to skip rope.

grounding: A grandmother recalls believing, at nine, that a radio toffee jingle was a real story that would win her company at school, until her Papa explained it was an advert.

passage:
The school bus would come in five minutes, and Harish had exactly twenty rupees for a compass.
But on the shop counter hung the chips packet with the famous cricketer, smiling right at him. On TV, the cricketer opened a packet and the stadium cheered. Inside was a player card. Everyone in Class 4 was collecting them.
"Ankita didi, just this one," Harish begged. "Then I'll be in the card group."
Ankita looked at the bus road, then crouched down. "That cricketer is paid to hold the packet, Harish. It's an advert, like a poster that talks."
"But he eats them."
"He's acting. Do the card boys play with you only because of cards?"
Harish thought about it. The bus horn sounded. He bought the compass.

qa.q: How much money did Harish have?
qa.a: Harish had exactly twenty rupees.

qa.q: How did Harish feel about the chips packet, and why?
qa.a: Harish felt eager to belong, believing the packet's player card would get him into the card group, so it meant belonging, not just chips.

qa.q: How did Ankita support Harish in the short time before the bus?
qa.a: Ankita crouched down and explained simply that the cricketer was paid and acting, then asked a question that let Harish think it through himself.

qa.q: What would be different if Ankita had just said no without explaining?
qa.a: Harish might still believe the advert was real and feel he had lost his chance to belong, instead of starting to see how ads work.

grounding: A young boy wants chips a cricketer sells on TV because he thinks they will bring belonging, and Ankita didi explains what an advert is.

passage:
During the cartoon break, Kunal's favourite jungle hero popped up on the TV, crunching a packet of orange chips. "Every packet has a hero sticker! Join the Jungle Gang!" Kids on the screen laughed and high-fived.
Kunal, eight, bounced on the sofa. "Yamini didi, if I get those, I'll be in the Jungle Gang too!"
Yamini, who was fifteen, muted the TV. "Kunal, that bit isn't the cartoon. It's an ad. The chip company paid to put the hero there so kids would want the packet."
Kunal frowned. "But it was the same hero."
"Same drawing, different job," she said. "Tomorrow at the shop, let's look at the packet together and see what's really inside."

qa.q: What did the ad say was in every packet?
qa.a: Every packet has a hero sticker.

qa.q: Why did Kunal bounce on the sofa during the ad?
qa.a: Kunal felt excited and hopeful, believing the chips would make Kunal part of the Jungle Gang like the laughing kids.

qa.q: How did Yamini help Kunal understand the ad?
qa.a: Yamini muted the TV, explained that the chip company paid for the hero to appear, and planned to look at the packet together at the shop.

qa.q: What would change if Yamini had not been in the room?
qa.a: Kunal might have kept thinking the ad was part of the cartoon and begged for chips to join the gang, with nobody to explain the difference.

grounding: Shows a young child wanting chips because a cartoon hero promises belonging, and an older sister explaining that it is an ad.

passage:
"Baba, I need the Thunder bat. The one the cricketer uses in the ad."
"You have a bat, Arnab."
"But in the ad, when he hits with it, the whole stadium jumps. And all the boys in the ad get picked for the team."
Zubin, Arnab's older cousin, looked up from his book. "Do you think the bat made the stadium jump?"
Arnab thought. "Maybe?"
"He gets paid to hold it," Zubin said. "Like the milkman gets paid to bring milk."
"Baba, is that true?"
"It's true," Baba said. "The ad is made to make you want it. It isn't a real match."
Arnab looked at his old bat with its taped handle. "So Thunder won't get me picked?"
"Practice will. Want to bowl to me after dinner?"
Arnab was already running for the ball.

qa.q: What did Arnab say happens in the ad when the cricketer hits?
qa.a: When he hits with it, the whole stadium jumps.

qa.q: What did Arnab hope the Thunder bat would bring?
qa.a: Arnab was hopeful and excited that the bat would make Arnab like the boys in the ad who get picked, so the wish was about belonging more than the bat.

qa.q: How did Baba and Zubin help Arnab see the ad differently?
qa.a: Zubin asked whether the bat made the stadium jump and compared the cricketer to someone paid for a job; Baba confirmed it and offered practice instead.

qa.q: What is it like for Baba when Arnab asks 'Baba, is that true?'
qa.a: Baba is being trusted to explain what Arnab cannot yet tell alone, so a calm, honest answer and an offer to bowl matter more than a flat no.

grounding: Shows a child wanting a bat because a cricketer's ad promises being picked, and adults in the family explaining that it is paid advertising.

passage:
I'm Zubin. Last year I saw an ad for Robo-Racer every single afternoon. The kids in it were at a big party, and the kid with the robot was the boss of everyone. I thought if I had one, Amandeep and the others would always want to come over.
I asked for it on my birthday, and I got it. It ran into the wall twice and then the battery died.
Amandeep came over anyway, like always, and we played cricket in the corridor.
Later Mummy sat with me and paused the ad on her phone. "See, the party kids are actors. The toy is small, but the camera is very close." Now I look for the tiny words at the bottom of ads.

qa.q: What happened to the robot after Zubin got it?
qa.a: It ran into the wall twice and then the battery died.

qa.q: What did Zubin hope the robot would bring?
qa.a: Zubin was hoping to feel included and liked, believing the robot would make the others always want to come over.

qa.q: How did Mummy help Zubin understand the ad?
qa.a: Mummy paused the ad and showed that the party kids were actors and the camera made the small toy look big.

qa.q: What does Amandeep coming over anyway show?
qa.a: Amandeep came over like always, so the friendship never depended on the robot; the belonging the ad promised was already there.

grounding: Shows a child believing a toy ad promised friends and fun, and a parent helping the child see how the ad was made.

passage:
Teacher's note, Class 2, Friday.
At show-and-tell, Dilnaz brought an empty snack packet with a cartoon tiger on it. She said, "If you eat these, you get lots of friends, like in the video." Three others nodded; they had seen the same advert. When I asked what the video was for, Dilnaz said it was "a story about the tiger".
I didn't laugh. We looked at two adverts together on the smartboard and talked about who made them and why: to make us want to buy. Dilnaz asked, "So the tiger doesn't give real friends?" I said friends come from playing together, not from a packet. She thought about it, then asked Meenu to play tag.
I will send a short note home suggesting parents talk about adverts too.
Pallavi

qa.q: What did Dilnaz bring to show-and-tell?
qa.a: An empty snack packet with a cartoon tiger on it.

qa.q: What did Dilnaz believe the snack would bring?
qa.a: Dilnaz felt hopeful and sure that eating it would bring lots of friends, and thought the advert was a story about the tiger.

qa.q: How did Pallavi help the children understand adverts?
qa.a: Pallavi didn't laugh; the class looked at two adverts, talked about who made them and why, and heard that friends come from playing together.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz's parents help at home?
qa.a: They could talk about adverts while watching together, so Dilnaz learns to ask who made them and why.

grounding: Shows a young child believing an advert means a snack brings friends, not yet able to tell an ad from a story, and an adult explaining.
